expectedText:
DISPOSITION OF REMAINS INSTRUCTIONS
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Lee

DESIGNATION OF AGENT TO CONTROL DISPOSITION OF REMAINS
I, Jordan Alex Lee, being an adult of sound mind, direct under California Health & Safety Code §§ 7100 and 7100.1 that Morgan Lee shall have the right to control the disposition of my remains, including the location and conditions of interment and arrangements for funeral goods and services, ahead of any person who would otherwise hold that right under the statutory order of priority. If Morgan Lee is unable, unwilling, or unavailable to act, I designate Casey Lee to act in Morgan Lee's place. This document revokes any earlier written direction I have given under Health & Safety Code § 7100.1 regarding the disposition of my remains.

DEFAULT PRIORITY ORDER FOR CONTROL OF DISPOSITION
California Health & Safety Code § 7100(a) provides that, unless other directions have been given by the decedent under Health & Safety Code § 7100.1, the right to control the disposition of a decedent's remains, the location and conditions of interment, and arrangements for funeral goods and services — together with the corresponding duty and cost liability — vests in the following persons, in the order named: (1) an agent under a power of attorney for health care with the right and duty of disposition under Probate Code Division 4.7 (commencing with § 4600), whose personal liability for costs is limited to cases where the agent specifically agreed to pay them or personally incurred them through the agent's own decisions; (2) the competent surviving spouse; (3) the sole surviving competent adult child, or a majority of the surviving competent adult children if there is more than one; (4) the surviving competent parent or parents; (5) the sole surviving competent adult sibling, or a majority of surviving competent adult siblings if there is more than one; (6) the surviving competent adult person or persons in the next degree of kinship, or a majority of persons of that same degree; (7) a conservator of the person appointed under Probate Code Division 4, Part 3 (commencing with § 1800), if the decedent has sufficient assets; (8) a conservator of the estate appointed under the same provisions, if the decedent has sufficient assets; and (9) the public administrator, if the decedent has sufficient assets. For categories (3), (5), and (6), the statute allows less than a full majority to act if they used reasonable efforts to notify the others and are not aware of opposition from the majority. As written, category (2) names only a "competent surviving spouse" — the text does not itself say "or registered domestic partner."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) The right to control the disposition of the remains of a deceased person, the location and conditions of interment, and arrangements for funeral goods and services to be provided, unless other directions have been given by the decedent pursuant to Section 7100.1, vests in, and the duty of disposition and the liability for the reasonable cost of disposition of the remains devolves upon, the following in the order named:(1) An agent under a power of attorney for health care who has the right and duty of disposition under Division 4.7 (commencing with Section 4600) of the Probate Code, except that the agent is liable for the costs of disposition only in either of the following cases:(A) Where the agent makes a specific agreement to pay the costs of disposition.(B) Where, in the absence of a specific agreement, the agent makes decisions concerning disposition that incur costs, in which case the agent is liable only for the reasonable costs incurred as a result of the agent's decisions, to the extent that the decedent's estate or other appropriate fund is insufficient.(2) The competent surviving spouse.(3) The sole surviving competent adult child of the decedent or, if there is more than one competent adult child of the decedent, the majority of the surviving competent adult children. However, less than the majority of the surviving competent adult children shall be vested with the rights and duties of this section if they have used reasonable efforts to notify all other surviving competent adult children of their instructions and are not aware of any opposition to those instructions by the majority of all surviving competent adult children.(4) The surviving competent parent or parents of the decedent. If one of the surviving competent parents is absent, the remaining competent parent shall be vested with the rights and duties of this section after reasonable efforts have been unsuccessful in locating the absent surviving competent parent.(5) The sole surviving competent adult sibling of the decedent or, if there is more than one surviving competent adult sibling of the decedent, the majority of the surviving competent adult siblings. However, less than the majority of the surviving competent adult siblings shall be vested with the rights and duties of this section if they have used reasonable efforts to notify all other surviving competent adult siblings of their instructions and are not aware of any opposition to those instructions by the majority of all surviving competent adult siblings.(6) The surviving competent adult person or persons respectively in the next degrees of kinship or, if there is more than one surviving competent adult person of the same degree of kinship, the majority of those persons. Less than the majority of surviving competent adult persons of the same degree of kinship shall be vested with the rights and duties of this section if those persons have used reasonable efforts to notify all other surviving competent adult persons of the same degree of kinship of their instructions and are not aware of any opposition to those instructions by the majority of all surviving competent adult persons of the same degree of kinship.(7) A conservator of the person appointed under Part 3 (commencing with Section 1800) of Division 4 of the Probate Code when the decedent has sufficient assets.(8) A conservator of the estate appointed under Part 3 (commencing with Section 1800) of Division 4 of the Probate Code when the decedent has sufficient assets.(9) The public administrator when the deceased has sufficient assets."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7100(a), complete statutory priority list for the right to control disposition of remains (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7100.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's default priority scheme for who has the legal right and duty to control disposition of a decedent's remains — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's remains, or that any other state orders priority the same way; both the identity and order of persons on this list vary significantly by state. The statutory text itself names only a "competent surviving spouse" in category (2); it does not say "or registered domestic partner." Whether a registered domestic partner is treated the same as a spouse for this specific list would depend on Family Code § 297.5's general rule equating domestic partners with spouses for most purposes, which has not been independently verified against this specific section as part of this research. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 7100(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

A DECEDENT'S WRITTEN DIRECTION CAN OVERRIDE THE DEFAULT ORDER
California Health & Safety Code § 7100.1(a) lets a competent adult, prior to death, direct in writing the disposition of the person's remains and specify the funeral goods and services to be provided — and § 7100(a) makes the entire statutory priority order it sets out apply only "unless other directions have been given by the decedent pursuant to Section 7100.1," so a validly made § 7100.1 direction by Jordan Alex Lee would supersede the default priority list. For Jordan Alex Lee's direction to be binding as written and not subject to alteration by anyone else, two conditions must both be met: the directions must set forth Jordan Alex Lee's final wishes clearly and completely enough to preclude any material ambiguity, and arrangements for payment (through a trust, insurance, a commitment by another person, or any other effective and binding means) must have been made so that no survivor who would otherwise hold the right to control disposition is left to pay for it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) A decedent, prior to death, may direct, in writing, the disposition of his or her remains and specify funeral goods and services to be provided. Unless there is a statement to the contrary that is signed and dated by the decedent, the directions may not be altered, changed, or otherwise amended in any material way, except as may be required by law, and shall be faithfully carried out upon his or her death, provided both of the following requirements are met: (1) the directions set forth clearly and completely the final wishes of the decedent in sufficient detail so as to preclude any material ambiguity with regard to the instructions; and, (2) arrangements for payment through trusts, insurance, commitments by others, or any other effective and binding means, have been made, so as to preclude the payment of any funds by the survivor or survivors of the deceased that might otherwise retain the right to control the disposition."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7100.1(a), a decedent's written direction on disposition of remains, and the conditions for it to be binding (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7100.1.)
  "The right to control the disposition of the remains of a deceased person, the location and conditions of interment, and arrangements for funeral goods and services to be provided, unless other directions have been given by the decedent pursuant to Section 7100.1, vests in, and the duty of disposition and the liability for the reasonable cost of disposition of the remains devolves upon, the following in the order named:"
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7100(a) [opening clause], the default priority order yields to a decedent's § 7100.1 direction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7100.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's mechanism for a person to set binding advance instructions on the disposition of their own remains — not a claim about which state's law would govern, or that another state uses the same mechanics; some states use a distinct "designation of agent" form with its own execution formalities, and California's approach here is different. Unlike the separate route of naming an agent under a power of attorney for health care (which Probate Code § 4673 requires to be notarized or signed by two qualifying witnesses), the text of § 7100.1 itself imposes no notarization or witness requirement — its only stated conditions are the clarity/completeness of the instructions and that funding arrangements have been made; this has not been cross-checked against any individual funeral establishment's own paperwork practices, which may go beyond what the statute requires. The statute's own words say a decedent may "direct... the disposition" and "specify funeral goods and services" — it does not use the word "agent" or expressly say the decedent may name a substitute decision-maker; that it also functions as a way to name a specific person (rather than only set instructions) is inferred here from § 7100(a)'s cross-reference making the default order yield to "other directions... given... pursuant to Section 7100.1," not from explicit statutory language using the word "agent" or "designate."

DISPOSITION INSTRUCTIONS AND PREFERENCES
My preferences and instructions regarding disposition of my remains, given under Health & Safety Code § 7100.1, are as follows:

Method of disposition: ☐ Burial ☐ Cremation ☐ Other: _________________________

Specific instructions: I wish to be cremated and my ashes scattered at a location of my agent's choosing.

Funding arrangements made for these costs (trust, insurance policy, prepaid contract, or other binding means): Prepaid funeral contract #1234 with Acme Mortuary

These instructions are intended to set forth my final wishes clearly and completely, and are to be carried out to the extent funding has been arranged for them as described above.

HOW FAR A WRITTEN DIRECTION MUST BE FOLLOWED WHEN FUNDING IS INCOMPLETE
California Health & Safety Code § 7100.1(b) addresses what happens if a decedent's written direction only arranged payment for one of the two cost categories — either the cost of interment or the cost of the funeral goods and services — rather than both: the remaining, unfunded wishes are carried out only to the extent the decedent's estate has sufficient assets to pay for them, unless the person or persons who would otherwise have held the right to control disposition agree to assume that cost themselves. All other provisions of the direction — the ones for which funding was arranged — must still be carried out.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) In the event arrangements for only one of either the cost of interment or the cost of the funeral goods and services are made pursuant to this section, the remaining wishes of the decedent shall be carried out only to the extent that the decedent has sufficient assets to do so, unless the person or persons that otherwise have the right to control the disposition and arrange for funeral goods and services agree to assume the cost. All other provisions of the directions shall be carried out."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7100.1(b), proration when only one cost category is funded (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7100.1.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of how one state prorates the enforceability of a decedent's own funeral/disposition instructions when funding was only partly arranged — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's estate, or that other states apply the same partial-funding rule. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 7100.1(b)); no additional independent source was found for this specific point.

A DISPOSITION DIRECTION PLACED IN A WILL TAKES EFFECT IMMEDIATELY, WITHOUT WAITING FOR PROBATE
California Health & Safety Code § 7100.1(c) provides that if a decedent's written direction on disposition of remains is contained in a will, it must be carried out immediately upon death — regardless of whether the will is otherwise valid, and regardless of whether the will has yet been offered for or admitted to probate. The statute addresses only that timing question; it does not separately state which document controls when a will's disposition instructions and a standalone, non-will disposition-of-remains document conflict with each other.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(c) If the directions are contained in a will, they shall be immediately carried out, regardless of the validity of the will in other respects or of the fact that the will may not be offered for or admitted to probate until a later date."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7100.1(c), a will-based direction is carried out immediately, regardless of probate status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7100.1.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's rule that a will's disposition-of-remains instructions are not held hostage to the probate timeline — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's remains, or that every state treats a will's disposition clause the same way. As to whether a later, separate § 7100.1 document overrides an earlier will provision on the same subject, or vice versa, no statutory text answering that question was found anywhere in this chapter; § 7100.1(c) only removes the probate-timing objection to a will-based direction and does not rank a will against a non-will writing when the two conflict. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 7100.1(c)); no additional independent source was found on the priority question, and it should be treated as an open point rather than a settled one.

HOW A DISPOSITION DIRECTION CAN BE CHANGED OR REVOKED
California Health & Safety Code § 7100.1(a) states that, once made, a decedent's written direction on disposition of remains "may not be altered, changed, or otherwise amended in any material way, except as may be required by law," unless the person who made it has signed and dated a statement to the contrary. The statute does not set out a separate, dedicated revocation procedure of the kind that exists elsewhere in California law for revoking an agent designation in an advance health care directive; the only mechanism the text of § 7100.1 itself describes for changing a direction is the maker's own signed and dated statement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless there is a statement to the contrary that is signed and dated by the decedent, the directions may not be altered, changed, or otherwise amended in any material way, except as may be required by law, and shall be faithfully carried out upon his or her death..."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7100.1(a) [revocation], the only stated method for altering a written direction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7100.1.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's limited statutory text on altering a disposition-of-remains direction — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's document, or that every state handles revocation the same way. This is the same subsection already quoted for the written-direction mechanism (§ 7100.1(a)); no additional independent source or separate revocation-specific statute was found in this chapter, and the practical mechanics of superseding an earlier § 7100.1 document — for example, by simply executing and dating a later one — are not spelled out beyond this sentence. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 7100.1(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

NO SEPARATE STATUTORY PRIORITY RULE FOUND FOR ALREADY-CREMATED REMAINS
California Health & Safety Code § 7100(a)'s priority-of-control framework, on its face, governs "the disposition of the remains of a deceased person" generally, without carving out a separate rule for who controls remains after cremation has already occurred, as distinct from the initial decision to cremate. Health & Safety Code § 7112 addresses cremated remains, but on two narrower points that are not about who controls disposition: it bars any action against a cemetery authority over cremated remains left in its possession for a year (unless there is a written care contract or the remains have been permanently interred), and it states that a licensed funeral director is not liable in damages for the lawful disposition of cremated human remains. Neither provision assigns or re-orders the right to control what happens to cremated remains once cremation has taken place.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The right to control the disposition of the remains of a deceased person, the location and conditions of interment, and arrangements for funeral goods and services to be provided, unless other directions have been given by the decedent pursuant to Section 7100.1, vests in, and the duty of disposition and the liability for the reasonable cost of disposition of the remains devolves upon, the following in the order named:"
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7100(a) [opening clause, cremated], the general disposition-of-remains framework, with no cremated-remains carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7100.)
  "No action shall lie against any cemetery authority relating to the cremated remains of any person which have been left in its possession for a period of one year, unless a written contract has been entered into with the cemetery authority for their care or unless permanent interment has been made.No licensed funeral director shall be liable in damages for the lawful disposition of any cremated human remains."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7112, cremated remains — retention-period and lawful-disposition liability rules only (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7112.)
  Known gap: This is a negative finding about California's statute, reported directly rather than forced into a citation that doesn't support it: a review of the entire Health & Safety Code chapter governing custody and duty of interment (§§ 7100-7117.1) did not turn up a separate, clean statutory provision assigning the right to control already-cremated remains distinct from the general § 7100(a) priority framework that governs "remains" generally; § 7112's cremated-remains language is a liability/retention-period rule, not a control-priority rule. This does not rule out that such a rule exists elsewhere in California statute or case law outside this specific chapter — only that it was not located within the disposition-of-remains chapter itself, which is where it would be expected to appear.

LIABILITY PROTECTION FOR A FUNERAL DIRECTOR, CEMETERY AUTHORITY, OR CREMATORY THAT RELIES ON THE DESIGNATION
California Health & Safety Code § 7100(f) states that a funeral director or cemetery authority is not liable to any person for carrying out the instructions of the decedent or of the person entitled to control the disposition. Separately, Health & Safety Code § 7111 lets a cemetery authority or crematory proceed with an interment or cremation upon receiving a written authorization from a person who represents that they have the right to control disposition under § 7100, and shields the cemetery authority or crematory from liability for cremating, interring, or otherwise disposing of remains in reliance on that authorization — unless it has actual notice that the representation is untrue.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(f) A funeral director or cemetery authority shall not be liable to any person or persons for carrying out the instructions of the decedent or the person entitled to control the disposition."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7100(f), no liability for carrying out the decedent's or controlling person's instructions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7100.)
  "A cemetery authority or crematory may make an interment or cremation of any remains upon the receipt of a written authorization of a person representing himself or herself to be a person having the right to control the disposition of the remains pursuant to Section 7100.A cemetery authority or crematory is not liable for cremating, making an interment, or for other disposition of remains permitted by law, pursuant to that authorization, unless it has actual notice that the representation is untrue."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7111, good-faith reliance on a written authorization of right to control disposition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7111.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's rule protecting a funeral director, cemetery authority, or crematory that relies in good faith on a decedent's instructions, the statutory default order, or a person's written representation of authority under § 7100 — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific facility's conduct, or that every state extends the same good-faith reliance protection to funeral or cemetery businesses. § 7100(f) and § 7111 are genuinely different statutory sections, not two subsections of one section, so they are treated as independent sources here.

SIGNATURE AND NOTARIZATION
Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

California Health & Safety Code § 7100.1 does not itself require this document to be witnessed or notarized. Some funeral establishments and cemetery authorities may nonetheless request notarization or witnesses as their own condition for accepting a written authorization under Health & Safety Code § 7111.

Optional notary acknowledgment:

State of California, County of _________________________

On _________________________, before me, personally appeared Jordan Alex Lee, proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence to be the person whose name is subscribed to this instrument.

Notary signature: _________________________ Printed name: _________________________ Commission expires: _________________________
